{"id": "101:7/q08", "question": "What makes the scales heavy and brings the pleasing life?", "turns_on": "What is credited with weight: good deeds, the monotheistic confession, God's decree, or inward spiritual attainment.", "positions": [{"id": "101:7/q08/p1", "position": "Abundant good deeds outweigh evil and bring salvation or lasting Paradise bliss.", "reasons": "Qushayrī says the scales are heavy with good deeds. Iṣlāḥī says only deeds help on that Day and a just, special balance weighs them; 21:47 is cited. Kur'an Yolu says abundant good earns God's approval and rich Gardens. Qāshānī says enduring righteous deeds weigh more than perishable pleasures; he rejects a preceding annihilation reading as unfit for the heavy/light distinction. The light-scale counterpart has little good according to al-Qummī."}, {"id": "101:7/q08/p2", "position": "Sincere monotheism, expressed in the confession that there is no god but God, makes the scales heavy.", "reasons": "Muqātil says only sincere monotheists reach this outcome and remain satisfied in Paradise."}, {"id": "101:7/q08/p3", "position": "God makes scales heavy or light according to His will and pre-eternal decree.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī answers a question about whether deeds cause the weight by citing a report that the scales are in God's hand and He raises or lowers people."}, {"id": "101:7/q08/p4", "position": "Real sciences and perfections of the psyche, heart, and spirit constitute weight.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says ascent in God's scale is weight and descent is lightness; enduring righteous deeds matter, whereas passing pleasures have no weight. The ensuing life is in gardens of attributes above gardens of deeds."}]}
{"id": "101:7/q09", "question": "What is weighed, and how is the weighing understood?", "turns_on": "Whether the weighing concerns deeds directly, their records, or corresponding created substances; the mode of an unseen event is also disputed or withheld.", "positions": [{"id": "101:7/q09/p1", "position": "Deeds themselves are what the scales weigh.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī describes a just, special balance for human deeds and cites 21:47. Kur'an Yolu prefers mawāzīn as the things weighed, namely deeds; it also reports the plural of mīzān, scales, as a metonym for those deeds. Its author cautions that the actual method is unseen and cannot be speculated about."}, {"id": "101:7/q09/p2", "position": "The written records of deeds are weighed.", "reasons": "Qushayrī reports this as one account of how deeds are weighed."}, {"id": "101:7/q09/p3", "position": "Created substances corresponding to each component of one's acts are weighed.", "reasons": "Qushayrī reports that their weight provides the measure of deeds."}, {"id": "101:7/q09/p4", "position": "The actual way deeds are weighed cannot be specified beyond revelation.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says events of the afterlife are unseen and one may not speculate about their measurement."}]}
{"id": "101:7/q10", "question": "How does this promise connect with the opposite fate in the adjacent verses?", "turns_on": "How the verse's positive clause is matched against the light-scale clause: direct contrast, ellipsis, or support for a particular reading of its wording.", "positions": [{"id": "101:7/q10/p1", "position": "The passage contrasts the reward of heavy scales with the fate of light scales.", "reasons": "Ālūsī says it divides people into two groups after describing what is common to all. Study Quran identifies the final six verses as this contrast. Iṣlāḥī says good outweighing evil brings bliss and the reverse Hell; al-Qummī glosses light scales as little good."}, {"id": "101:7/q10/p2", "position": "The contrast permits an omitted hostile life in the second clause and an omitted mother in the first.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reads Hāwiya at 101:9 as a low descending fire in which its inhabitant keeps falling, against the lofty pleasing life here."}, {"id": "101:7/q10/p3", "position": "The forceful description of the pleasing life favors reading the later Hāwiya wording as an imprecation.", "reasons": "Al-Kashf calls that later reading best for matching the preceding emphatic life; al-Ṭībī calls it clearest, while Ālūsī leaves the argument open."}]}
{"id": "101:7/q11", "question": "What other Quranic wording is linked to this pleasing life?", "turns_on": "Which shared expression or subject is being cross referenced.", "positions": [{"id": "101:7/q11/p1", "position": "The expression is paralleled by 69:21, with 88:9 also noted.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān twice sends readers to his treatment of the expression at 69:21; Study Quran links the contenting life to that verse. Corpus Coranicum adds 88:9 and observes early Meccan r-ḍ-y usage at 93:5, 92:21, 89:28 and 53:26, with an apparently consistent eschatological association. Mujāhid's and Qatāda's reports in Ṭabarī's full text also mention 69:21."}, {"id": "101:7/q11/p2", "position": "Discussion of the scales here is referred to 7:8–9.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān directs the reader to his earlier treatment of heaviness and lightness in al-Aʿrāf."}]}
{"id": "101:7/q12", "question": "What place does this verse have in the sūra's wider presentation?", "turns_on": "The notes address different aspects of the same sūra: resurrection and chronology versus its question structure.", "positions": [{"id": "101:7/q12/p1", "position": "The Meccan sūra warns of resurrection while giving glad tidings, with warning dominant.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes the overall theme; Asad calls the sūra early Meccan and probably later than al-Tīn (95), adding a chronological estimate."}, {"id": "101:7/q12/p2", "position": "The sūra uses riddling teaching questions to build rhetorical tension.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares the questions in 101:1–11 with 90:12–16, 97:2–4 and 104:5–9, and with an oath sequence in Q 100."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q01", "question": "What are the mawāzīn, and what is weighed?", "turns_on": "Whether mawāzīn names an actual instrument, weighty deeds, or a figure for judgment, and whether deeds themselves can be weighed.", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q01/p1", "position": "A real balance weighs deeds or their written records at the Resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya attributes a balance with a beam to most scholars, jurists, and hadith scholars, saying its familiar form makes divine judgment intelligible and trusted. Ibn Abbas in Razi describes a tongue and two pans: beautiful obedient deeds outweigh and lead to Paradise, whereas ugly unbelievers' deeds are light and lead to Fire; al-Hasan affirms two pans without further description. Qurtubi specifies written records of good and bad deeds on a pan and tongue and refers to earlier discussions. Study Quran distinguishes Qur'anic balance as revelation and just order (6:152, 7:85, 11:84–85, 42:17, 55:7–9, 57:25) from scales for deeds at Resurrection (21:47). Islahi calls it a just balance of deeds."}, {"id": "101:8/q01/p2", "position": "Mawāzīn are deeds that possess weight and worth before God.", "reasons": "Al-Farra in Razi treats mawāzīn as a plural of mawzūn and compares ordinary expressions about one thing being the measure or weight of another. Kashshaf gives this as an alternative to weighing scales. Tabatabai assigns weight and standing to faith and obedience, and none to disbelief and sins; Qutb speaks of values with no weight in God's assessment."}, {"id": "101:8/q01/p3", "position": "The scale is a metaphor for divine justice.", "reasons": "Mujahid in Ibn Atiyya denies a literal balance because the scale is the fairest familiar measure. The representative form of weighing conveys just judgment in Kuranyolu's account."}, {"id": "101:8/q01/p4", "position": "The balances are proofs and arguments.", "reasons": "Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya in Qurtubi cites a poet speaking of a balance for every disputant."}, {"id": "101:8/q01/p5", "position": "What is weighed may be records or visible representations of deeds, since vanished deeds cannot themselves be weighed.", "reasons": "The theologians reported by Razi object that deeds, especially after ceasing to exist, cannot be weighed. Their alternatives are weighing records, light and darkness denoting good and evil, or records embodied in beautiful and hideous forms, publicly disclosing each person's standing."}, {"id": "101:8/q01/p6", "position": "The actual manner of weighing is beyond specification from revelation.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says afterlife events are unseen and one cannot speculate beyond what revelation states about how deeds are weighed or measured."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q02", "question": "Why is mawāzīn plural and assigned to a person?", "turns_on": "Whether the grammatical plural reflects multiple objects, multiple instruments, or individual experiences despite one instrument.", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q02/p1", "position": "The plural covers the many different things belonging to a person that are weighed.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya explicitly explains the plural and the possessive in this way."}, {"id": "101:8/q02/p2", "position": "There are multiple balances.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports this interpretation and cites a poet's line that every event has its balance."}, {"id": "101:8/q02/p3", "position": "A single balance, held by Gabriel, is expressed in the plural.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports the one-balance interpretation; Study Quran says most hold that one scale weighs all deeds despite the plural."}, {"id": "101:8/q02/p4", "position": "The plural evokes each person's experience of weighing.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this suggestion while noting the majority view of a single scale."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q03", "question": "What makes a person's scales light?", "turns_on": "Whether lightness describes the balance of bad against good, scarcity or loss of worthy good, following falsehood, or intrinsic lack of divine weight.", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q03/p1", "position": "Bad deeds outweigh good deeds.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Baghawi,

Razi, Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi, Elmalili, Islahi, and Kuranyolu give the comparative account; Razi and Kuranyolu add that good deeds are few. Biqai calls the scales light or unsteady. Bursevi says both groups sin, but the blessed have fewer, outweighed sins; he cites the Prophet's instruction to Ali to follow a bad deed with a good one and God's forgiving name. Islahi says this outcome leads to Hell under God's just balance."}, {"id": "101:8/q03/p2", "position": "The person followed light falsehood instead of weighty truth.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls truth heavy and wholesome and falsehood light and vile; Abu Bakr in Wahidi, Kashshaf, and Razi relates their weight to following them in worldly life and says a scale holding only truth should be heavy and one holding falsehood light. Nasafi and Biqai attribute lightness to following falsehood; Biqai adds it felt light in worldly life. Islahi says only truth, meaning good deeds, has weight, and connects loss to denial of God's revelations (7:8–9)."}, {"id": "101:8/q03/p3", "position": "There is no good deed of consequential weight.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi, and Elmalili give this as an alternative to bad deeds outweighing good; Biqai links the lack to following falsehood. Kuranyolu allows few or no good acts. Qutb says values without weight have no standing in God's judgment."}, {"id": "101:8/q03/p4", "position": "Good deeds and obedience are few or scarce.", "reasons": "Tabari says the good deeds weigh little; Tabrisi says few good deeds and little obedience. Ibn Atiyya says faith and deeds make a balance heavy and absence or scarcity makes it light. Razi and Kuranyolu combine few good deeds with wrongs outweighing them."}, {"id": "101:8/q03/p5", "position": "Shirk or corrupt belief nullifies the good deeds, leaving nothing weighty.", "reasons": "Muqatil says shirk's good deeds turn to wind-scattered ash; shirk is the foulest yet lightest thing in the balance. Islahi says any good deeds are voided by ill intent and heretical belief, while evil deeds carry no weight."}, {"id": "101:8/q03/p6", "position": "Disbelief and sins have no weight before God, unlike faith and obedience.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says deeds are weighed by their standing with God; faith and obedience have weight and bring felicity, while disbelief and sins lack it and bring misery. Qutb describes the light scales as values without weight in divine assessment."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q04", "question": "Whose scales can be ruinously light?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse identifies unbelief as the condition of ruin or states a general bad-over-good criterion.", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q04/p1", "position": "The disbelievers, especially those whose shirk or denial voids their good deeds.", "reasons": "Qushayri identifies those light in obedience as disbelievers; Muqatil names shirk and its wind-scattered good deeds; Islahi links the loss to denying revelations and to ill intent and heretical belief. Ibn Atiyya says a believer's balance is never disastrously light, a point repeated in Ibn Atiyya Full."}, {"id": "101:8/q04/p2", "position": "Anyone whose bad deeds exceed their good deeds is in the light-scale group.", "reasons": "The general descriptions by Wahidi, Baghawi, Razi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi, Alusi, and others state the bad-over-good criterion without restricting the wording to a named people. Bursevi says both groups commit sins, though in the blessed group sins are fewer and outweighed."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q05", "question": "How does the singular man refer to those being weighed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q05/p1", "position": "The singular relative expression denotes a plural group.", "reasons": "Islahi explicitly notes the singular man in the two scale descriptions has plural reference."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q06", "question": "What outcome follows light scales?", "turns_on": "Whether the following image emphasizes the abiding destination or the manner of falling into it.", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q06/p1", "position": "The person's abode or destination is Hawiya, the Fire or Hell.", "reasons": "Tabari says the person of scant good deeds has Hawiya as abode. Thalabi, Qushayri, Qatada in Tabari and Durr, and Kuranyolu identify the destination as Hell or Fire; Durr's versions call it abode, mother, destination, and master. Biqai describes a very low fiery abyss; Islahi says the next verse names it blazing fire and calls the punishment eternal."}, {"id": "101:8/q06/p2", "position": "They plunge headfirst into Hell.", "reasons": "Tabari reports Abu Salih and Qatada saying they fall headfirst into Fire, and Tabari himself includes that descent; Thalabi attributes the head interpretation to Qatada and Abu Salih. Ikrima in Mawardi identifies the mother as the head and cites a poem addressed to Amr."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q07", "question": "Why is the following Hawiya called the person's mother?", "turns_on": "Whether mother names a sheltering destination, the head of the falling person, or an idiom of calamity.", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q07/p1", "position": "Hell is the person's refuge and return, like a child's mother or one's home.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd in Tabari and Mawardi says Hell is refuge and return, citing 3:151 and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's poem; Ibn Abbas says it is the only home and shelters the person as a woman shelters her child. Biqai likens the shelter to a mother or the earth to which one returns; Qatada in Durr calls it abode, mother, destination, and master. Tabari records a report from al-Ashath about believers' spirits saying the dead were taken to their mother, Hawiya."}, {"id": "101:8/q07/p2", "position": "Mother means the person's head, upon which the person falls.", "reasons": "Thalabi reports this interpretation from some, attributing its adoption to Qatada and Abu Salih. Ikrima in Mawardi describes the fall on the head and supports the image with a poem addressed to Amr."}, {"id": "101:8/q07/p3", "position": "It is a familiar Arabic exclamation for someone in severe trouble.", "reasons": "Qatada in Tabari and Thalabi explains hāwat ummuh or hawat ummuh as idiomatic speech about a person in dire predicament; Tabari also reports the wording hāwat ummuh directly."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q08", "question": "Why is the Fire called Hawiya?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q08/p1", "position": "It is an abyss into which the person falls through deep reaches.", "reasons": "Mawardi derives the name from falling into it despite its deep abyss. Biqai depicts the sinner continually falling through its depths and describes it as very low and fiery."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q09", "question": "What reports illustrate the weighing and its result?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different illustrations or qualifications of the weighing, rather than competing versions of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q09/p1", "position": "An angel weighs each person's deeds and announces lasting felicity for a heavy scale or lasting misery for a light one.", "reasons": "Thalabi transmits this from Anas ibn Malik, including the public proclamation."}, {"id": "101:8/q09/p2", "position": "A margin of one good deed brings Paradise, and a margin of one bad deed brings Hell.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits this statement from Ibn Masud."}, {"id": "101:8/q09/p3", "position": "A huge, tall, voracious man can weigh no more than a gnat's wing before God.", "reasons": "Abd al-Razzaq reports this saying of Ubayd ibn Umayr."}, {"id": "101:8/q09/p4", "position": "No thing put in the Balance weighs more than good character.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this hadith."}, {"id": "101:8/q09/p5", "position": "Deeds are judged by intentions and each person receives what was intended.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the Prophet's hadith."}, {"id": "101:8/q09/p6", "position": "No one, even the Prophet, enters Paradise by deeds alone, but through God's mercy.", "reasons": "Study Quran quotes the Prophet's answer that only God's mercy would shelter him."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q10", "question": "What principles govern the moral weight and recompense of deeds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q10/p1", "position": "Faithful obedience and good deeds have standing; disbelief and sins have none.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says faith and obedience bear weight before God and lead to felicity, while disbelief and sins lack weight and lead to misery. Islahi makes truth or good deeds alone weighty and attributes the light scale to denial of revelations (7:8–9)."}, {"id": "101:8/q10/p2", "position": "Good deeds can erase evil and are rewarded tenfold, while evil is repaid only in kind.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 41:34 and 11:114 for overcoming and erasing evil and 6:160 for the unequal recompense."}, {"id": "101:8/q10/p3", "position": "Only deeds help at judgment, and the just balance calls for responsible belief and conduct.", "reasons": "Islahi says God weighs deeds in a just balance, with eternal bliss or Hell according to which side prevails. Kuranyolu calls the scene illustrative imagery that teaches just judgment and responsible conduct and belief."}, {"id": "101:8/q10/p4", "position": "A deed's intention affects its value.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the Prophet's saying that deeds are judged by intentions; Islahi says ill intent and heretical belief nullify otherwise good deeds."}, {"id": "101:8/q10/p5", "position": "Divine mercy is needed for entry to Paradise even when deeds are weighed.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the Prophet saying that no one enters through deeds alone, including himself; only God's mercy shelters him."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q11", "question": "What inward meaning is given to light and heavy scales?", "turns_on": "The inward notes apply weight to spiritual ascent and lasting traits and lightness to veiling, appetite, and descent.", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q11/p1", "position": "Spiritual ascent and enduring righteousness are he

Bursevi also says God's scale reverses ordinary scales: enduring good works rise, whereas passing sensual pleasures have no value."}, {"id": "101:8/q11/p2", "position": "Light scales are psychic vices and evil deeds, ending in the hell of bodily nature and spiritual veiling.", "reasons": "Qashani makes bodily nature's abyss the owner's home. The Najmi interpretations cited by Bursevi describe a hot fire of ignorance, blindness, ego, passion, Satan, and the world."}, {"id": "101:8/q11/p3", "position": "Godly attributes and character bring rest from the consequences of those qualities.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this from the Najmi interpretations for the person whose weighed qualities are divine attributes and godly traits."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q12", "question": "How does the verse fit the surrounding passage and sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q12/p1", "position": "The Resurrection scene divides humanity into heavy and light scale groups with opposed outcomes.", "reasons": "Razi says God divides people after describing Resurrection; Alusi says the passage first describes what all share and then each group's state. Study Quran says the final six verses contrast good-deed-heavy and light scales. Tabatabai says the Meccan sura warns and promises about resurrection, with warning dominant."}, {"id": "101:8/q12/p2", "position": "The ending with the wretched prepares the next sūra's warning about the cause of misery.", "reasons": "Biqai says al-Qaria first establishes the Hour and divides happy and wretched, ends with the wretched, and then the next sura opens with what caused that misery (101:1, 101:8–9; 102:1)."}, {"id": "101:8/q12/p3", "position": "The passage uses a teasing question and delayed explanation to create rhetorical tension.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares the teaching questions of 101:1–11 with 90:12–16, 97:2–4, and 104:5–9, and with oath sequences such as Q 100."}, {"id": "101:8/q12/p4", "position": "The opposed destinies are expressed with antithetical omitted clauses.", "reasons": "Biqai points to antithetical ellipsis in the clauses around the sinner's refuge."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q13", "question": "What other Qur'anic passages are linked to this verse's weighing and outcome?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q13/p1", "position": "The light scales and abyss are paralleled in 7:9 and 23:103.", "reasons": "Study Quran names both parallels; Islahi cites 7:8–9 for the balance in which truth has weight and deniers lose."}, {"id": "101:8/q13/p2", "position": "Earlier passages explain the weighing, and 69:21 describes the pleasing life of the other group.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan points back to discussion at 7:8 and to Sura al-Haqqa's pleasing life at 69:21. Tabatabai likewise says the scale has been explained under earlier suras."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q14", "question": "When was the sūra containing this verse revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q14/p1", "position": "It is a Meccan sūra.", "reasons": "Tabatabai describes its Meccan setting and its dominant resurrection warning; Asad calls it early Meccan and tentatively places it after al-Tin (sura 95)."}, {"id": "101:8/q14/p2", "position": "It was probably revealed after Sūrat al-Tīn.", "reasons": "Asad gives this tentative placement for the early Meccan sura, citing sura 95."}]}
{"id": "101:8/q15", "question": "What does the omitted adjective imply about the scales' weight?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:8/q15/p1", "position": "The implied weight is one of value; omitting an adjective magnifies the noun.", "reasons": "Burhan says omission of an adjective often magnifies an indefinite noun and that the implied weight here is one of value."}]}
{"id": "101:9/q01", "question": "What does ‘his mother is Hawiya’ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether umm denotes an abode by maternal analogy, the top of the head, the actual grieving mother in an idiom, or the sinner's origin; the following feminine pronoun and Arabic idiom/poetry are used to decide.", "positions": [{"id": "101:9/q01/p1", "position": "His final abode and only refuge is Hell, called his mother as a child returns to and shelters with its mother.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls it his origin and abode: neither earth bears him nor sky shades him; he compares umm al-qura (6:92). Al-Farra, Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Abbas, al-Akhfash, Abu Ishaq and others explain a mother's shelter, nurture, feeding, dwelling or place of return. Ibn Qutayba compares figurative father language for God's mercy and Jesus' water and bread as parents, rejects a biological reading, and cites the Arab name mother for earth as origin, return and sustenance; Umayya's poem calls earth mother and refuge. Ibn Atiyya cites Utba's battle saying about earth as mother. Tabari cites 3:151 for the Fire as abode. Al-Akhfash cites a poem about a fallen mother; al-Nahhas also cites mother of the Qur'an and a poem for origin/core. Ibn Kathir reports the two principal interpretations without choosing. Alusi and Bursevi add that the analogy can taunt and that Fire encloses the sinner like a womb; Kuranyolu depicts Hell opening its arms. Asad says umm is what embraces or enfolds, Study Quran derives it from amma, directing one's course, and Elmalili calls the refuge metaphor painfully ironic. Biqai notes earth and dwelling are called mother because they embrace and shelter. Qutb says partial obscurity heightens the later disclosure. Al-Tabatabai calls it a rational metaphor. Al-Nasafi and al-Wahidi stress a mother's place of rest. The Fire is the only remaining shelter, not a literal parent. Damghani explicitly lists destination among five senses of umm, alongside origin, biological mother, wet nurse and the Prophet's wives. Itqan classifies Hell's motherhood as figurative, modeled on a human mother's literal sheltering of her child, and compares fire's figurative 'calling'."}, {"id": "101:9/q01/p2", "position": "‘His mother’ is his head or crown: he is cast headfirst into Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalid/Abu Khalid al-Walibi glosses umm as the crown or top of the head. Ikrima, Abu Salih, Qatada, Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi and others describe the headfirst plunge, sometimes to the bottom of Hell. Al-Mawardi cites a poem addressed to Amr; al-Nahhas reports the related fallen-mother poetic line. Ibn Kathir allows head or brain; Bursevi specifies umm al-ra's as brain or its thin covering. Ibn Ashur supplies the ellipsis umm ra'sihi and treats hāwiya as fallen, likening a fall on the crown to death. Elmalili gives either brain's root as Hawiya or a headfirst fall. Al-Qummi calls Hawiya the head itself. Al-Tabatabai objects that this leaves the next verse's feminine pronoun without an apparent antecedent."}, {"id": "101:9/q01/p3", "position": "The phrase invokes the Arabic idiom ‘his mother fell’: he is ruined, with his mother imagined collapsing in grief at his death.", "reasons": "Qatada and Ibn Abbas cite hawat/hawiyat ummuhu for grave calamity; al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, Alusi and others explain the imagined bereavement. The idiom can be a curse, an omen, wonder or even praise of brave dead warriors: Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi and the Hamasa poet supply examples, as do an unnamed poet and a line about morning and night. Ibn Ashur compares thakalathu ummuhu, explains the ellipsis and detached min in Ka'b's elegy, and sees reuse of a fixed expression for an analogous fate; he also illustrates how Arabs depict fortune through a mother's joy with a Bedouin's remark about Abraham (4:125). A report about la umma laka is linked to this verse. Al-Kashf and al-Tibi praise this reading for its relation to the earlier satisfied life (101:7); Elmalili notes its subtle force but favors the refuge reading. Corpus Coranicum reports Fischer's preference and lexical evidence, but objects that the following teaching question normally points to the named Hawiya; Fischer's proposed later addition of verses 10–11 is called unsupported. It allows an echo of the idiom alongside a real abyss."}, {"id": "101:9/q01/p4", "position": "‘Mother’ marks the Fire as the sinner's origin or native element, because he was created from or dominated by a fiery nature.", "reasons": "Biqai says the image suggests creation from Hell and a satanic, fiery nature. Bursevi says the fire-created unbeliever returns to his origin and calls this explanation apparent; he also lists refuge, taunt and womb-like enclosure."}]}

{"id": "101:9/q04", "question": "What does the following ‘what is it?’ refer to, and how does this verse prepare its answer?", "turns_on": "Whether the feminine pronoun has the named Hawiya as its concrete antecedent or must recover calamity, Fire, or the preceding sentence from an idiomatic/head reading.", "positions": [{"id": "101:9/q04/p1", "position": "The pronoun refers to Hawiya; its initially obscure threat is explained as blazing Fire in verses 10–11.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Alusi and Elmalili point the pronoun directly to Hawiya. {"id": "101:9/q05", "question": "What is the final ha in the following question?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:9/q05/p1", "position": "The final ha is a pausal letter, omitted by some in connected recitation and retained by others in agreement with the written codex.", "reasons": "Kashshaf gives the alternatives while discussing the following question's pronoun."}]}
{"id": "101:9/q06", "question": "What does the verse imply about the light-scale person's fate and deeds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:9/q06/p1", "position": "The person with light scales has Hell as the destination, because good deeds are too few or outweighed by evil.", "reasons": "Tabari says good deeds weigh little and the person falls into Hell; Qushayri identifies the disbelievers whose obedience is light. {"id": "101:9/q07", "question": "What inward reality does the abyss represent?", "turns_on": "The inward accounts specify different contents of the light-scale person's abyss: corporeal nature or veiling and ignorance.", "positions": [{"id": "101:9/q07/p1", "position": "The abyss is the hell of bodily or corporeal nature for a person ruled by evil deeds and psychic vices.", "reasons": "Qashani places the light-scale person's home in bodily nature's hell. {"id": "101:9/q08", "question": "What do reports about souls say about being taken to Hawiya?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:9/q08/p1", "position": "Believing souls welcome a new believer and ask about others; a person who died earlier but has not joined them was taken to mother Hawiya.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan transmits a Prophetic version calling Hawiya a wretched mother and nurse; al-Ash'ath transmits the exchange. {"id": "101:9/q10", "question": "Why use this word and this compact wording?", "turns_on": "The notes offer rhyme and antithetical ellipsis as distinct explanations of the wording.", "positions": [{"id": "101:9/q10/p1", "position": "The rare word Hawiya helps preserve the sura's rhyme.", "reasons": "Itqan says the Qur'an often chooses rarer synonyms, listing dayza, al-Hutamah, Saqar, Laza and Hawiya, in part for each sura's rhyme. {"id": "101:9/q11", "question": "How does this ending connect to the sura and its neighbors?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "101:9/q11/p1", "position": "The sura moves from the Hour to two opposed outcomes and ends with the wretched; the next sura opens with the cause of their misery.", "reasons": "Biqai relates 101:1, 101:8–9 to the opening of sura 102. {"id": "102:1/q01", "question": "What does أَلْهَىٰكُمُ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is rendered by its ordinary effect, distraction, or by the alluring manner of that diversion.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q01/p1", "position": "It occupied, distracted, or made you forget what matters.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī derive it from turning away or forgetting; Ibn Fāris calls anything occupying one lāhī. {"id": "102:1/q02", "question": "What did rivalry distract people from?", "turns_on": "Whether the unspoken object is read broadly or supplied specifically from the audience and context.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q02/p1", "position": "Obedience, worship, remembrance of God, and preparation for the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Muqātil says remembrance of the afterlife; al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī and others say obeying God and escaping His anger. Al-Biqāʿī adds death and saving acts; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies hearing Qurʾānic evidence and accepting the Prophet's call. 63:9 is used for the warning (Jishumī); al-Qāriʿah and the scales ground it for al-Biqāʿī and Elmalılı. Zayd b. Aslam transmits in a mursal report a prophetic expansion that rivalry distracts from obedience."}, {"id": "102:1/q02/p2", "position": "The omitted object allows every important concern neglected by diversion.", "reasons": "Rāzī says an absolute construction intensifies blame; al-Biqāʿī says omission magnifies the importance of what is neglected, and Elmalılı notes both distraction's object and accumulation's kind are unstated."}, {"id": "102:1/q02/p3", "position": "In its immediate address, it diverted polytheist chiefs from Qurʾānic guidance and fair acceptance of Muhammad's call.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr infers the object from the wealthy chiefs' choice of luxury and their obstruction of others; past tense presents this distraction as already accomplished."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q03", "question": "Why is the object of أَلْهَىٰكُمُ unstated?", "turns_on": "Whether ellipsis deliberately leaves all neglected duties open or expects a definite object to be inferred.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q03/p1", "position": "Its omission broadens and intensifies the rebuke.", "reasons": "Rāzī says an absolute construction lets the mind supply every neglected object: remembrance, duties, recommended acts, knowledge and reflection. {"id": "102:1/q04", "question": "How is أَلْهَىٰكُمُ read and what force does the opening have?", "turns_on": "The transmitted opening hamza and whether an assertion or question better conveys the rebuke.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q04/p1", "position": "It is a declarative statement of an actual distraction, used as censure.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān attributes the statement to the majority. {"id": "102:1/q05", "question": "What does ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether form VI names mutual boasting, acquisitive increase beyond boasting, or a possible Greek-derived expression.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q05/p1", "position": "Mutual boasting and rivalry in having more people, possessions, or valued distinctions.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba names people and kin; al-Kashshāf and al-Ālūsī say each group claims numerical superiority. {"id": "102:1/q06", "question": "What does the form of ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ express?", "turns_on": "Which attested force of form VI is active in this context.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q06/p1", "position": "It expresses reciprocal boasting, each party claiming more.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists reciprocity among the possible senses of tafāʿala; Rāzī and Bursevī describe rival groups or individuals comparing wealth and followers."}, {"id": "102:1/q06/p2", "position": "It can express determined effort to increase or acquisition of quantity, without reciprocal boasting.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim lists effort and an intransitive increase alongside reciprocity; Rāzī applies effort to the ambitious pursuit of wealth. {"id": "102:1/q07", "question": "What kind of abundance or pursuit is meant by ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ?", "turns_on": "Whether the unrestricted noun points to all worldly increase or to a particular object established by a gloss, report, or occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q07/p1", "position": "Worldly abundance broadly, including wealth, children, people, status, allies, and pleasures.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿĀshūr hold wealth and numbers together; Rāzī lists money, ranks, kin, supporters, armies, every pleasure. {"id": "102:1/q10", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported?", "turns_on": "The differing transmitted reports identify distinct communities, and some describe a literal graveyard count while others describe dying during rivalry.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q10/p1", "position": "Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Sahm of Quraysh competed in numbers and notables, then counted the dead.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Sahm exceeded ʿAbd Manāf by three households; al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān report ʿAbd Manāf led among the living but Sahm among the dead because of larger pre-Islamic numbers. {"id": "102:1/q11", "question": "How does the following grave visitation complete this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the next clause describes literal counting at graves, death in figurative language, or a visit that prompts reflection.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q11/p1", "position": "The rivals counted or named dead ancestors at the graves to extend a contest begun among the living.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf calls 'visiting' sarcastic; Abū Ḥayyān calls it a mocking depiction.
